lines: THE TRIAL OF ELSIE LANSING WHIPPLE
The court re-opened this morning at 10 o'clock, at which time both Mrs. Whipple and Strang were brought into court.
Present:
His honour William A. Duer,
their honours the Mayor and Recorder,
and Aldermen Treat and Esleeck.
Counsel for the prosecution,
District Attorney Edward Livingston,
and S. A. Foot.
Counsel for the prisoner, Abraham Van Vechten, Williams, and Tabor.
Mrs. Whipple, as before, was deeply veiled. Strang's deportment was grave, and one would suppose that his feelings had been somewhat softened.
He was brought in for the purpose of being used as a witness. His father accompanied him, and sat down by his side, and they were for some time engaged in conversation.

Elsie D. Whipple was then placed at the bar, and the clerk commenced drawing a jury. She was attended by some relations, and one of them, Dr. Killian Van Rensselaer Lansing, who has never left her in court a moment, but has manifested the greatest tenderness and solicitude for her throughout, took a seat by her side.

She was requested to rise, and have her veil raised, that she might "look upon the juror," and the juror upon the prisoner. Her appearance was interesting, and there was much sympathy for her wretched situation apparent throughout the crowd.
After several hours passed in challenging, the jury was completed, as follows, viz:
Henry Cornelius, of Knox;
Fathao Elliott, of Westerlo;
J. B. Crouse, of Bethlehem;
Henry Devine, of Guilderland;
Henry Ketchum, of Knox;
John Reid, William Gardiner; and Wilhelmus Winne, of Bethlehem;
Philip Eagle, of Berne;
Alexander Schoonmaker, of Knox;
John Geddes, of Watervleit;
Philip Crounce, of Guilderland.
All were farmers by occupation.
The court here remarked, that it was hardly deemed admissible at this late hour in the afternoon, to commence a trial of so much magnitude.

And as it was hoped that they would be able to go through with the whole of it in one day, it was thought best to direct a recess until 9 o'clock tomorrow morning, when court, counsel, jury and all, could enter upon their duties with bodies and mind much refreshed.
—Four constables were then sworn to take charge of the jury, keep them together, and provide for them comfortable refreshment and lodging.
THE PEOPLE v. ELISE WHIPPLE
Court of Oyer and Terminer
Present—His honor Wm. A. Duer, their honors the Mayor and Recorder, Treat and Alderman Esleek.
Counsel for the prosecution, Edward Livingston, District Attorney, and S. A. Foot.
For the prisoner, Van Vechten, Williams, and Tabor.
The Court having taken their seats at 9 o’clock, Judge Duer, briefly stated to the jury the nature of the charge which they were impannelled to try.
The prisoner having been placed at the bar, and Strang having been brought into court and seated back as yesterday, and the jury having been called over, the proceedings were resumed as follows:
By the Court.

Gentlemen of the Jury, the prisoner at the Bar, Elsie D. Whipple, stands indicted for a felony for having been accessory before the fact, to the murder of her husband, the late John Whipple. This indictment will be read to you by the District Attorney, before any further proceeding.
Mr. Livingston then read the indictment.

To this indictment, gentlemen, the prisoner has pleaded "Not Guilty," and put herself upon God and her country for trial—which country you are. She is to receive at your hands a fair and impartial trial. Mr. Livingston then rose and opened the cause to the jury with much candor and perspicuity.
Mr. Livingston then opened the case at some length.

Mr. Livingston commenced by expressing his sincere regret that his public duty imposed upon him the necessity of presenting a case of the peculiarly aggravated character of the one now before the court. The prisoner is charged with one of the blackest and most atrocious crimes presented in the dark catalogue of human frailty and human guilt.

It is alleged in the indictment, that she aided, abetted, and procured the murder of her husband by the hand of Jesse Strang—that husband to whom she was bound by the strongest ties, and whom she had sworn at the altar to love, honor and obey.

Yet the duty so imposed upon me, however painful, is one, the faithful discharge of which, the public have a right to expect and demand. The prisoner is a lady, of extensive and respectable connections, who has been blessed with all those early advantages in life which it is in the power of wealth to bestow.

Under these circumstances, the base thought that such a crime could have been deliberately perpetrated by her aid and connivance, is enough to make us shudder: and yet, she is entitled to no more favor or commisseration, than the most poor and the most humble.

“It is, however,” said Mr. Livingston, “a source of peculiar pleasure to me, that her wealth, and the influence of her family connexions, have enabled her to bring to the work of her defence, an array of the most ingenious, able and powerful counsel in the land. And happy should he feel, if by the exertions of such talents, she could consistently with the demands of public justice, be saved from condemnation.

“On the part of the people,” said Mr. Livingston, “we shall be content to rely upon the strength of the testimony: and if it lie not sufficiently strong of itself, resist the combined assault which will be made upon it, by the experience and learning of the one, and the commanding eloquence, ingenuity, and forcible pleadings of the other of her counsel, we neither wish nor expect a verdict at your hands. But although the counsel for the prisoner exceed us in professional rank, yet it will be found that our duties are also unequal. “

While they are bound to exert the full force of their talents in the defence of their client, we shall think our duty discharged by eliciting a fair, full, and impartial statement in evidence, of all the facts in the case.

“And here, gentlemen,” said Mr. Livingston, “let me assure you, that did we even possess the powers of swaying the passions and feelings, of which the counsel for the prisoner may justly be proud, yet we should feel it unjustifiable to exert them on such an occasion.

Turning, however, from the counsel opposite, to the court, my satisfaction is increased, by the consideration that the court will guard her rights from invasion; and should any thing material to her defence be omitted on the part of her counsel, the court, according to the humane principles of the law, will consider themselves also counsel for the prisoner.

But all fear of the prisoner’s being wrongfully convicted is banished from my mind, when I reflect, that the issue in which the prisoner’s life is at stake, is committed for decision to an intelligent and impartial jury of the county of Albany, indifferently chosen, tried, and sworn, to pass between the people and the unfortunate woman at your bar.

“In conducting this prosecution, I trust that I shall be found utterly incapable of pressing upon your attention any fact or circumstance which may be developed in testimony more strongly than may be strictly warranted by its character.

If any lingering prejudices should remain upon your minds, I conjure you to dismiss them, by the fearful responsibility of the obligation which you have taken upon yourselves, and prepare your minds to receive the testimony, unbiased and uninfluenced by any of the stories which the lovers of the marvellous have set afloat in relation to this transaction.
You will bear in mind gentlemen, that persons about to commit a crime of the enormity charged in the indictment, would naturally seek to envelope it in darkness.

You will not, therefore, expect higher testimony than the nature of the case affords. Its perpetrators would not do the foul deed until they had employed every artifice and device, which would be calculated to elude suspicion.

And experience, drawn from the history of cases of this kind, tell us, that you will generally find that the murderer and his accomplices have previously fortified themselves with circumstances to prove their innocence, with all the cunning and assiduity of cowards.

This case you will find strongly marked with indications of this description. You will, therefore, perceive, from the very nature of the charge, that unless some misunderstanding has taken place between its authors, or some accidental circumstance has exposed their conduct, we must necessarily rely upon circumstantial testimony.

[Here Mr. Livingston dwelt briefly upon the nature of testimony of that character, and said that it often afforded a more sure guide to truth, than the positive testimony of witnesses, as witnesses may perjure themselves, and that circumstantial testimony cannot lie.]

But in addition to the train of circumstances which he supposed implicated the prisoner, Mr. Livingston said, he should offer the principal in guilt, (Jesse Strang) who was convicted of having murdered Whipple, as a witness to prove the agency of the prisoner in this transaction.
[Mr. Livingston then stated the law applicable to the case, and gave a brief outline of the facts upon which he would rely, to sustain the charge made in the indictment.]

He said in conclusion, that he hoped the jury would give a strict and undivided attention to every word that might fall from the mouth of the witnesses, as every word, and even the manner in which they give in their testimony, might have an important influence in swaying their judgments in the conclusion to which they might come.

Life and death are in your hands, and you are bound to dispense them under the sanction of your oaths. If the guilt of the prisoner shall not be clearly established, if she shall be able satisfactorily to explain away the circumstances which militate against her: or, if you should have a reasonable doubt upon the testimony before you of her guilt, it will be your duty to acquit her; all, or either of which, I humbly hope and trust, she will be able to make appear to the satisfaction, not only of you, gentlemen, of the court, and of those assembled on this occasion, but of the whole of this community.

But if, on the other hand, from the testimony, you should believe her guilty, I trust you will perform your duty with firmness, and say so; remembering that you have the high sanction of the Court of Heaven, which has proclaimed, that he who sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed.
Abraham Van Rensselaer, sworn.

Witness stated that Strang first came to his father’s house on the 28th August last, as a laborer. He represented himself as a single man. Mr. and Mrs. Whipple were there as boarders in the family. About the first of May, Whipple was absent, down the river. He had been absent about two weeks previous to the 7th of May.

He and his wife occupied on the 7th, and some time previous, the south west bedroom in the second story. When Whipple was absent, the other females of the family slept with Mrs. Whipple. Henrietta Patrick generally slept with her.

Whipple was killed on Monday night. Does not know whether the family expected him home at the time he arrived. It was not known at what time he would come. Was in the room in which he was shot on the night of the 7th. Mrs. W. was there also.

Does not know exactly how long it was before he was shot that she left the room. Does not know what she had been doing in the room previous to her leaving it. Does not remember that she said anything of a pistol at that time. Believes that there were other members of the family in the room at the time.
Cannot say who they were. There might have been several persons there. Miss Patrick and his sister.

There were several alarms given by Strang, as to persons lurking about the house. [The testimony on this subject was the same as on the trial of Strang.] There had been alarms about the house for a fortnight before the murder of Whipple, in consequence of the declarations of Strang as to people being lurking about the house. Strang told witness that he thought those people had designs upon Whipple. Did not recollect exactly what prisoner said when Strang told her of these things. Did not remember any statements of the prisoner to Strang, when he remarked that the persons about the house meant no good to Mr. Whipple.
Heard prisoner state that she was going to write to Mr. Whipple.

This was a few days before the murder. She was in the cellar-kitchen at the time. Understood that she intended to write a letter and leave it at the Columbian Hotel, warning John not to come home at night, because some person lurking about the house would rob him. Did not hear her say afterwards that she had written such a letter.
On the day previous to the evening of the murder, the prisoner borrowed a pencil of the witness. She also asked for a piece of paper.
This was in the afternoon, at three or four o'clock. She went to a window, where she had a book of her own. Does not know whether she did write or not.
Mr. Van Vechten moved that Strang be removed out of hearing of the testimony, to which the court acceded, and he left court in care of an officer.

Witness proceeded. Lent the pencil to the prisoner in the kitchen. Don't know positively whether she wrote with the pencil or not. Thinks he saw her at the window in a writing position; can hardly say he did. His mind was so agitated when he gave that affidavit, that he hardly knows what he deposed. Is pretty sure she was in a writing position at the window. Strang was in the kitchen while she appeared to be writing.

The prisoner and Strang passed by each other continually in the kitchen that afternoon. Shortly after he saw the prisoner writing, Strang left the kitchen. It was not more than fifteen minutes after. Witness went out soon also; perhaps five or ten minutes after Strang. Found Strang a little south of the kitchen door, standing near a wagon.
His back was towards witness. He had a paper in his hand, and was tearing it. It was a piece of paper. Could not say how large it was. Does not remember ever to have seen the fragments on the ground.

Was at home on Wednesday night, the ninth of May. Don't recollect any examination having been taken on that night. Recollects having a conversation with Mrs. Whipple as to his having been examined—Thinks it was shortly after the murder.

She asked witness what was the meaning of cross-examination. Cannot tell exactly when this conversation took place. Believes that in that conversation she asked him whether he had been examined. Thinks she asked him whether all the family had been examined or were to be examined. Cannot recollect whether they had been. Does not know what answer he gave to the question.
She asked also whether Orton had been examined. Strang went at that time by the name of Orton.
Does not know whether Strang had been arrested at that time. He was arrested on Wednesday afternoon.

When Mrs. W. asked the question the police officers had been down and examined the family, or were examining them. In the night, a day or two after the murder, when witness had been in bed and asleep, in a bed-room, adjoining the room in which Mrs. Whipple and his sister Maria were, his sister came into the room, and Mrs. Whipple after her. Mrs. Whipple said, that Orton had not yet come home, and asked whether it could be that he had been examined and cross-questioned, and "differed any."

She said, she "felt so bad, that she could take a knife and stick herself to the heart." This was what he recollected, although he was very sleepy. Does not recollect any remark of her's as to Orton's having spoken of her.
She never said any thing about witness' taking care of her son Abraham; and he does not recollect that she ever said there was property enough for her son.
She asked witness whether he had examined Strang's trunks, and what they had found in them. Told her that they found clothes and a bottle of rum.

This was after witness came out of the room into which the trunks had been carried to be examined. She asked whether they had found five hundred dollars there. She or his sister asked him if any papers had been found in the trunks. Told her he believed there was a parcel of papers in the pocket-book.
On refreshing his memory—thinks he told them there were no papers in the trunks. Does not know which of the females asked the question.
The mother was examined at the same time with the rest of the family. She was examined two or three times.

The prisoner fainted on the afternoon on which his mother was examined. She exclaimed, "Orton! Orton! My John! My John!" Thinks this was when Orton was taken to jail. It occurred in the cellar kitchen—she had fainted when witness come in. Several persons were present.

Believes the immediate cause of her fainting, was that Orton had been taken to jail. Believes that James Hoghkirk brought the news of Orton’s arrest, and told it to the family and to prisoner, and prisoner fainted some time afterwards.
Mr. Van Vechten said That the prisoner was indicted as an accessary in the murder of her husband; and the highest testimony was required to show that she was guilty.

He cited a case of murder, in which it was stated that the principal must be necessarily convicted before the trial of the accessary could proceed; and it was therefore requisite to commence with the preliminary testimony on record of the trial, and conviction of the principal.
This was essential, because if he had been acquitted, there could have been no trial of the accessary.
Until he was convicted, he could not be a witness—but the law involved such an absurdity, that he could become qualified to be a witness after conviction when he was not so before.
Had this been tried jointly, there would of course be no separate record; but their trials having been separate, there was a record in the case of Strang, and that must be proved.
Inferior evidence should not first be brought forward. The principal had been convicted; and it was said that his testimony would be produced.

But he was no longer worthy of credit, for the stain of infamy had been fixed upon him. It was argued that this infamy was withheld until sentence. This, however, could not be: it was not the sentence of the court which fixed the infamy.

Considerable argument took place between the counsel and the public prosecutor, on the admissibility of the Record, which occupied the Court until after one o’clock, when a recess was ordered for an hour and a half—Adjourned.
THE PEOPLE v. ELISE WHIPPLE

Judge Duer then gave the decision of the Court in the argument submitted. Our statute, which has been referred to, was, he considered, a transcript—and perhaps went further than the statute of Ann: and it was contended should extend beyond the cases in which principal and accessary are both tried.

We contend that it goes to the punishment not only as far as the guilt of the principal is shown, but to cases where the principal never can be convicted. On view of all the authorities, it was the decision of the Court that the trial of the accessary might be proceeded in, without waiting for the sentence of the principal.
Mr. Van Vechten wished the Court to make a note that an exception would be taken to this decision.
Mr. Foot stated, that, upon the record of conviction hitherto produced, it would be taken for granted that John Whipple was killed on the 7th May, and that Strang shot him with a rifle.
In the course of his remarks he stated that it was the intention of the counsel for the prosecution to produce Strang as a witness.
For doing so, Mr. Livingston observed there was authority, but more particularly a case in point which was tried in Orange County.

Among the various facts which Mr. Livingston. detailed as those which it was the intention of the prosecution to establish, was that of a correspondence having been kept up between the prisoner and Strang, down to the time of his imprisonment; and that on one occasion, when he is supposed to have been urging her to participate in the murder, she was heard to say, “John’s life (meaning her husband’s) is as dear to him as ours is to us,”—and that she said on the day of the murder, that she would write her husband, and warn him not to come home in the night, because some one intended to shoot him.

They should also show that, since Mrs. Whipple has been confined in jail, the jailor, through a motive of kindness, allowed the door of her apartment to remain open—permitting her to walk in the passage, and that she went repeatedly to the door of Strang, and lying down on the floor, held long conversations with him.

Most of the other facts which the prosecution stated as depended upon to convict the prisoner, were produced on the trial of Strang, or had some immediate connexion with the testimony given in that case.
Maria Van Rensselaer, sworn.

Thinks Mrs. Whipple was deranged during the night. Mrs. Whipple is sometimes subject to hysterics. She also appeared to be deranged on Thursday the day on which her husband was buried. Was partially so during a greater part of the week after the death of her husband.

Remembers the exclamations of Mrs. W. on the night on which Abraham was awakened. Thinks she was deranged at that time. She appeared so irrational that witness paid little attention to what she said. Recollects that she remarked that she had "lost her grand-father, and father, that now her husband lay a corpse, and that she should not live to see her son grow up." Mrs. Whipple is 25 years of age. She was married when she was a few months over fourteen. Witness’ father died last February. Mrs. W. is subject to occasional nervous affections, and will express her feelings by laughing and crying without apparent cause.
By Foot.

Mrs. Whipple. on the night of Wednesday, among other things in her derangement, said, “Tell me something that I know. Cross question me so that I may know.” She said also, “I am going to die to-night, and be buried with John. I am going to-night, and be buried to-night.”

Recollects no other words of Mrs. Whipple only these which she repeated after witness. Witness said to her brother that Orton not come home yet, and that his supper was waiting. This Mrs. Whipple repeated, after the witness. Either witness repeated the words, “What should keep him!” and Mrs. Whipple. said them after her, or Mrs. Whipple. said them of her own accord.

Did not particularly recollect any other declarations or exclamations of Mrs. Whipple than those stated. She spoke to Abraham about cross-questioning on the evening of the 9th. Considered this question to Abraham one of the manifestations of her being flighty. Her manner was abrupt and incoherent.

Her conduct in the afternoon denoted derangement. Her actions were different from what they had been before. Observed these strange actions after her coming out of the room where her husband’s body lay. This was about half an hour before she fainted. She spoke of her forlorn condition at that time, and said she had lost her only friend.

Almost impossible to specify the singular actions which appeared like derangement, and which were different from what they were before; but noticed them at the time. She spoke also in the afternoon, of her grandmother having died the week before.

She showed signs of insanity on Thursday, and spoke of having the grave made wide enough for her and her husband. Witness told her she acted as if she was crazy. She replied “I don’t know what I do know.”

At this time witness observed some singular actions. Witness limits her observations in relation to the insanity to Wednesday and Thursday. She might have been flighty after Thursday—and thinks she did act singularly. Prisoner was always subject to nervous affections, and her mother before her. Could not describe them; but when she was troubled she shewed it very plainly.

lines: THE PEOPLE v. ELISE WHIPPLE
The court meet at 9 o’clock.
One of the Jurors having complained of illness, Doctors Ray and Townsend were called, and administered to him in the box.
Mr. Williams applied to the Court to prevent any person having communication with Strang during the trial.
Some conversation then took place, which ended in a direction from the Court, that no one, with the exception of his counsel, his relatives, the jailor, and public officers, be admitted to him.
Gitty Sanford, sworn.

Knows the prisoner at the bar, and has known her from a little girl. Witness lived at the corner of Patroon and Pearl-streets. One day, some time in April, prisoner came to her house, about 4 o'clock, staid about an hour, and went away in a one-horse wagon. It was a green wagon.

There was a man whom she did not know, who had on a mixed coat. On the next morning, Mrs. Whipple came there again on foot, at about 8 o'clock, and said that she had been to Troy with Mr. Whipple's brother. She took breakfast with witness. On the first day, she appeared to be greatly troubled in mind.
Witness asked where she was going.—She said, "O my God, I am going a riding; I don't want to go, but if I don't go, the devil will kill me."

She said she was going to Troy with Mr. Whipple's brother. Did not say what they were going to Troy for. Witness thinks prisoner told her to keep her going a secret from her aunt, [Mrs. Van Rensselaer.] Said she was to return the next morning.
Frances Hill, sworn.
Her husband keeps a public house where the Albany and Niskayuna road crosses the Troy and Schenectady turnpike.
Witness described the visit of the prisoner with Strang, in April, on the day of the thunder storm, as during the trial of Strang. They staid that night, and witness lighted the pair to bed.
Witness, before lighting her to bed, asked if that man was her brother or her husband. She said he was her husband. There were two beds in the room, but only one had been tumbled the next morning.

Witness asked her the question whether Strang was her brother, because her parents thought she had better do it, they appeared to be so fond.—Witness likewise observed this fondness. She said they came from Schenectady, and were going to Albany and New-York. Is perfectly certain that the prisoner is the same woman.
Catharine Barringer, sworn.

On the 17th of April, witness resided at Mr. Hill's tavern. Prisoner came there that day with a man, whom she believed to be the person whom she had seen in court as Strang. They slept together. Witness passed through the room where they slept in the morning. Priso-ner was getting up. The man had got up before; only one bed however was tumbled. Witness had no conversation with her.
Matilda Becker, sworn.
Daughter of the Jailer, 13. Has known the prisoner ever since she came to the jail, and has slept in the room with her, since her confinement—has staid day and night with her.
Described the room in which she was kept, and also the room where Strang was.

The doors of both their rooms lead out into the same hall. Has not carried any notes or papers from prisoner to Strang, since she has been there. The prisoner has received papers from Strang since she has been there.

Witness thinks 2 or 3 times.—She brought the papers into the room herself, and believes they were shoved through to her under the door from Strang's room. She did not see the papers, and don't know that they came from Strang, but don't know how else she could have got them. The prisoner said she was going to Strang's door, and when she returned she had the papers.

Witness saw her have no papers before, and no other persons than Strang and Mrs. Whipple were confined in the third story. Witness saw prisoner at Strang's door once when she talked with him. She laid herself down by the bottom of the door, so as to talk with him through the crack underneath. She was there but a very few minutes.

Witness saw her at the door the first time she went there. She did not look after prisoner when she went there at other times, because she told her not to, as she might be used as a witness against her. Witness called her away from Strang's door once, and in doing so said, "she had better come away, as by and by somebody would come up and catch her there." This was the first time.
Henry Schoonmaker, sworn.

The Turn-key. He described the situation of the rooms in which Strang and prisoner were confined: there were two rooms between them. It was hot weather, about the 4th of July, and Mrs. Whipple's door was opened into the hall during the day, for several days, in order to give her the comfort of a free circulation of fresh air.

The next week after the 4th of July, the doors were closed, in consequence of information that Mrs. W. was in the habit of going to Strang's door and conversing with him. Witness has never heard any conversation between prisoner and Strang.—The aperture under his door was about an inch and a half wide. The length of Strang's chain would allow him to reach the door. Strang was furnished with pen, ink and paper.—Witness saw the copy of the National Observer newspaper in Strang's room.

There were some lines of poetry in the paper, a copy of which the witness has. Witness afterwards saw Mrs. W. have a written paper, but it was not the manuscript now in his hands. He did not see what was written on Mrs. Whipple's paper. The copy of verses which witness produced were copied from the National Observer, and the manuscript is the writing of Strang. Witness took it from the pantaloon's pocket of Strang.

A day or two after he saw the Observer in Strang's room, witness saw a piece of paper in Mrs. Whipple's room. Mrs. W. unfolded a part of the paper and read the lines. Witness first asked Mrs. W. to show him the lines. She refused to show them, but read a part. Witness told her he didn't care about her reading them, as he thought he had seen them before, in Strang's room, in the National Observer. She asked if Strang had shown them to him.

He told her that he believed Strang had copied them. She said she thought it was likely, as Strang did not know enough to compose such a piece of poetry as that. When witness first went into her room, before this conversation, prisoner told her that she had got a letter. He asked her where she got it, but she would not tell. He could not describe her manner—she talked freely, but did not act any way particularly unusual.
Philander Fobes, recalled.

On the day after the funeral, prisoner sent a message to witness, and wanted to see him. He went, and had a conversation with her. She said many things, and among others, remarked, that Strang applied to her to lend him sixteen dollars—she informed him that she had not got it nor any money, except a twenty dollar bill which she got of witness, or his bar-keeper.

Strang then said, if she would let him have the bill, he would pay her four dollars back, and the residue on Saturday night. She gave him the bill, and he gave her the four dollars then. But instead of paying her the sixteen dollars which he promised, he gave her only six. Thinks she told him that she gave Orton the twenty dollar bill on the same day that she got it of him.
Mary Heistick, sworn.

Prisoner was at the millinery shop of witness some time last winter. Prisoner came there to purchase some articles; she then sat waiting for a sleigh to take her home; had some conversation with her; told her it was cold, and she had better take a mantle, she said she should not be cold; she said she wished the doctor would come; did not know who she meant by doctor: she said he was coming with a load of wood, and she was going home on the wood sleigh; a man came for her, dressed in light gray; should not know him, but the prisoner went home with him on the wood sleigh; prisoner said she had a great deal of pleasure in coming down, but did not say how she came down.
Abraham Lansing Van Rensselaer, recalled.
—"Doctor" was a nick name which he had given Orton. Sometimes he was called Orton, and sometimes Doctor. Prisoner used to call him Doctor. Was in the habit of sending him to town with wood.
Henrietta Patrick, sworn.

Seamstress, niece of the deceased. Witness lived at Cherry Hill when the murder was committed, and before. The deceased, John Whipple, was her uncle. When he was absent witness slept with Mrs. Whipple. Strang sometimes came into the bed-room to make fires in the morning, but knows of no particular intimacy between prisoner and Strang.

About three weeks before the murder, witness found a paper under the pillow. It was burnt up by Maria Matilda Van Rensselaer. It was a kind of letter. Had read it. It was appointing a place to meet somebody at a small yellow house, to go to Lansingburgh.
Mrs. Whipple and Strang were both absent all night, one night in April. Mrs. Whipple told witness she was going, and requested her to meet her at Fobes the next morning at 12 o'clock.

She went and met her at a few minutes after 1.—Her appearance and spirits were as usual. Said she had weathered out the previous night with Miss Otis, up State street. She returned home about half past 11.

On the evening of the day when prisoner went out there was a very heavy thunder storm. Mrs. Whipple said she had slept at Fobes'. Did not understand that the paper found under Mrs. Whipple's pillow, was an answer to a proposition to go to Lansingburgh.

The words were, as near as she could recollect—"I will meet you at the yellow house, to go to Lansingburgh, in the north part of the city, and wait till I come." She went off in the afternoon of the same day on the morning of which witness saw the paper under her pillow. Witness thought "the yellow house" was near the patroon's bridge.

The note was found when the prisoner at the bar was preparing to go away. Maria Matilda was not present when witness found it. Did not converse with prisoner about it. The note was burnt that day, and was shown to none of the family but Maria Matilda. Witness asked prisoner where she was going, and she said she was going to Fobes' and should stay there all night.

Witness was at Cherry Hill when Whipple was murdered. When he was shot she was in the kitchen, (with same persons as were mentioned by Abraham L. Van Rensselaer, on the trial of Strang.) She heard a noise—then Mrs. Catharine Van Rensselaer shrieked—and Abraham Lansing Van Rensselaer came down, and said Whipple was shot thro' the head.

Two bed rooms were adjoining the kitchen—one occupied by Dinah (the servant) and the other by Strang.—When witness heard the noise, her first thought was that there were robbers about the house, and she ran into Dinah's room. Was there when Abraham told that Whipple was shot.

Mrs. Whipple was sitting on a bench by the fire, with a pipe in her hand, but does not know whether she was smoking or not.—Mrs. Whipple was more sociable with Strang than with the rest of the family. There was no member of the family so sociable with Strang as the prisoner. Does not know that Strang and the prisoner corresponded by letters.
Cross examined by Williams.

There were two beds in Mr. and Mrs. Whipple's room. When he was at home, he and his wife occupied one of the beds, and witness sometimes the other. Witness slept with the prisoner when her uncle was absent. Strang used to bring up wood into the room during the day, and make up a fire, whether Whipple was at home or not. Witness was in bed with Mrs. Whipple when Strang lighted her pipe. Mr. and Mrs. Whipple were to have started next morning after the murder to go down to Ulster county, where he had been on a contract on the canal.
Direct, by DA Edward Livingston.

Was in the kitchen on Wednesday the 9th May, when Mr. Cole was examining the witnesses. Recollects when Mrs. Catharine Van Rensselaer was examined. Mrs. Whipple fainted while Mrs. Catherine Van Rensselaer. was undergoing her examination. Was in the room when Mrs. Whipple first fainted.

She did not appear to be irrational at that time. Saw her on the evening after the murder. Cannot recollect how she appeared. Did not think on the afternoon of Wednesday that she was irrational. Took no notice of any very strange conduct in the prisoner. Saw nothing very unusual in the prisoner's manner on that evening, only that she had fainted, and did not feel well.

When Whipple was absent, thinks prisoner was called up once in the night to see little Abraham, her son, who slept below. Don't know who called her. She was gone perhaps half an hour. Mrs. Whipple did not tell witness what the matter was with Abraham.
THE PEOPLE v. ELISE WHIPPLE
Dinah Jackson, sworn.

Formerly enslaved, recently emancipated servant to the family at Cherry Hill testified that she heard Strang, a day or two before the murder, ask the prisoner to lend him a pair of socks; saw her go and get a pair of Mr. Whipple's white ribbed socks; saw them afterwards on Strang's feet in the forenoon of the day that Whipple was murdered; witness saw the prisoner and Strang talking together in a low voice in the kitchen; Strang was about the house, loading the wagon with potatoes.
Starr Foot, sworn.

About a fortnight before the murder, prisoner came to Fobe’s and asked witness if he had heard from Mr. Whipple? I answered, he had not. She then said there had been people seen lurking about the house; she could not think what they were there for, unless to waylay John (as she called Mr. Whipple) to kill him. She then said I will bet you a hat that he will be killed—and laughed. Witness asked, do you know anybody that is going to kill him? She answered, no; and witness observed to her it was a foolish remark, referring to what she had said. Nothing more was said; she went away; witness considered her in jest as to the offer of the bet.
Cross-examined.

Mr. Whipple's letters were usually left at Fobe's in his absence, unless sent for from Cherry Hill. During his absence, a letter was received, marked at New-Jersey; another from Vermont, and one left by Mrs. Whipple: On Monday in the forenoon, witness delivered the letters to Mr. Whipple; laid them down on the table; he took up the one written by Mrs. Whipple, tore it in two pieces without reading it and put it in his pocket. Witness asked him what he did that for? he said it was a letter that Mrs. Whipple wrote. He then read the letter from New-Jersey, and said here is a letter from New-Jersey, and they want me to repair a house there, but observed, the old lady never will die; I shall never get anything for it. He then read farther and said, she is dead, (alluding to the grandmother of prisoner.)

The letter from Mrs. Whipple was left on Thursday the 3d day of May, in the care of witness; it was written at Fobe's: when she came in she asked for $25 in money, which she wanted for her uncle, Dr. Lansing, who was repairing his house; had been disappointed and wanted money: there was not enough in the bar; witness called upon Mr. Fobe who gave him $25, and he gave it to Mrs. Whipple.

She then asked for writing materials: was in the sitting-room with Miss Patrick and Miss Otis: witness left them; when he returned she asked for a wafer which he procured and gave her; she then sealed the letter, and said "be sure to give it to him when he returns, and if he comes in the night, be sure and keep him all night and not let him come home," and again mentioned that people had been seen about the house; they did not know what they were there for, and she did not want her husband to come home in the night. She was not agitated when she spoke about the money; requested it should not be charged, and said don't let John know it, I will return it as soon as uncle repays it—asked for money with apparent unconcern.
Amanda Hill, sworn

Testified that she spent about four weeks at Cherry Hill last winter; while there, knew that the prisoner sent letters or papers to Strang, and Strang had sent papers or letters to the prisoner; had never had any particular conversation with the prisoner about Strang—did not know any thing about the contents of the papers. Witness once handed a paper to Strang at the request of the prisoner.

This was about the 1st of March. The paper was in the form of a letter, tho' she saw nothing written upon it. She received it in Mrs. W's room, when she was going down to the kitchen where Strang was. She had seen papers handed to the prisoner, who said they were from Strang.

She has seen this a number of times, but prisoner said nothing of the contents of the papers; had known of prisoner's reading papers to Strang two or three times: she had seen prisoner give letters to little Elsie Van Rensselaer, and heard her tell her to give them to Strang.

Saw no writing upon them, and knew nothing of their contents. She had seen little Elsie deliver letters to the prisoner several times. She does not recollect more than one time, when prisoner said they came from Strang. Witness did not read any of the papers. Never heard prisoner say she would not live all her days with Whipple that she had found the right man now. Witness lives in Sunderland, Vermont, and is a niece of the deceased.
Joel A. Wing, sworn
He was at Cherry-Hill on the 8th of May; went down at the request of the coroner to open the body of Whipple to extract the ball, and was there between 8 and 10 o'clock.

As he was about coming away, Abraham Lansing Van Rensselaer told witness Mrs. Whipple wanted to see him before he went away; found her in a room with several ladies; she wept violently, and her first expression was—"My dear, dear husband is dead;" the next expression was, "Doctor, I wish to see you"; she looked at the persons present, and said nothing more at the moment; witness inferred that she wished to communicate something to him, but wished to see him in private.

Witness took a seat near to her and sat a few moments, when some ordinary words passed about Mr. Whipple's death: she remarking, that she wished to communicate her suspicions of who had murdered her husband.

He told her he was ready to hear any thing she had to say: she again looked towards the company; upon which he told her he would call again next morning; prisoner said she wished he would; witness did not, however, see her again till Thursday morning, about 10 o'clock.

It was told to him as he approached the house, that Strang had been arrested; and suspicions were afloat that Mrs. Whipple knew something about it;—he had a conversation with Abraham L. Van Rensselaer on the subject, which determined him not to see the prisoner alone.

Prisoner commenced the conversation by saying, “Doctor, what do you think of this? I am accused of having something to do in the death of my husband. I wish I had been shot instead of him, for this is more than I can bear; she said, my aunt, my uncle Knickerbacker, and most of my relations, are bearing upon me, intimating that I have been the cause, or have been concerned in my husband's death.”

She said that every person seemed to have turned her enemy. “My aunt tells me that I am a very bad woman—that I am to be examined this afternoon, and that I may possibly be hanged; a gentleman came to me yesterday, while I was sitting in the room with my husband's corpse, and asked me if I would uncover his face and kiss it; she felt indignant, and asked the man if he thought she was afraid to kiss her own husband; that she then went to the corpse, put her arms about the neck and kissed it—and the man said, now I am satisfied. She did not say who the man was—she said Strang had been arrested as the supposed murderer. Witness then asked her who she supposed did it?

She answered, it was some person from Kingston, or New-York—for her husband had told her that he had had difficulty with some persons in regard to canal contracts in both places; said she could not see why they arrested Strang, because her husband had great confidence in him and had that morning hired him to go on the canal, and was to give him sixteen dollars a month instead of twelve, which he was then receiving.

Strang objected to going, because he had not proper clothes; when her husband told him to go up to town and purchase some, and if he had not money enough he would furnish him. Strang asked Henrietta if she could make a pair of pantaloons by the next morning at 9 o’clock; she said she could and he went up to buy cloth. She repeated that her husband had great confidence in Strang, and had much rather trust him in his business than a stranger.
She then said—"Doctor, if I am taken up and examined this afternoon, what will they say to me? what shall I say to them? or what will they do to me?"
Witness does not recollect which expression she used, but he replied, she had a plain course to pursue—she was as much or more than any one interested in finding out the murderer.

—She had better tell all she knew, and all she suspected. She said she should; “but how can I go through it? how can I bear this with all my other afflictions? my husband not yet buried, and all this put upon me?”
She burst into a flood of grief.—They were then interrupted by a lady, who burst rudely upon them, exclaiming—"well, my lady, well, Doctor, what do you think of her?

He supposed the lady who interrupted the conversation was the wife of Barnum Whipple; he had no acquaintance with her; has not seen her since, nor has he taken pains to ascertain who she was. Witness was deceased’s family physician.
The Court took a recess until half past three.
Calvin Pepper, sworn.

Witness was present when the rifle was found; he then waited till Strang, who had been sent for arrived, when he went with him to the place where the glass was found. Strang pointed out the place—fragments of glass were found about ten feet from a tree, which appeared to have been perforated by balls. The pieces of lead were cut out of the tree in presence of witness. Mr. Meigs picked up the pieces of glass; witness has not seen him since.

The trial was here interrupted for a short time by the sudden indisposition of a juror. Physicians were called—the juror was taken out in charge of officers, and walked about for air—restoratives administered, and in about half an hour, he was brought into Court, and the trial proceeded.
Melancton Whipple, sworn.

Testified, that he arrived in this city on the 5th of May, and saw John Whipple the 7th at dinner, at Fobes'. Heard of his uncle's death the next morning; went to Cherry Hill about 9 o'clock, when he saw the prisoner.

On Thursday, immediately after the funeral, he had a conversation with the prisoner; she came and sat down by the side of witness, and said to him, they say they have let Strang go, and taken up a man caught with no boots or shoes on.

Witness told her he thought not—that he did not think they would let him go very soon. She then said she expected to be sworn the next day, and should swear that he was innocent. He was one of John's best friends. This was all the conversation on that day.

Saw the prisoner the next day, but does not recollect that he conversed with her, but in the course of the next week, he saw her and conversed with her. At one time she said it was worse and worse; they had come there and taken one of John's best friends. Witness had some other conversations at different times, but does not recollect what they were.

At one time she told him about getting the money of Mr Fobes. and another time she said she had been told that Strang had said he had been somewhere and staid with her. If he had said so it was a lie—there was no such thing.

She once told him that Strang had lied, and would lie again: does not recollect that this was the time that they were talking about his having said that he had stayed with her; does not recollect any thing which followed this declaration, further than that she asked him whether if Strang was condemned, they would bring him to testify against her?

At one of the conversations, she told witness that Strang had told her that he would have her if it cost him his life, and that he proposed going to Canada: she said Strang had threatened to take the life of Whipple—cannot tell what day this conversation took place—but it was after the funeral.

At one of his visits, Mrs. Whipple took him into her bed-room, and had a long conversation with him. She said she had been examined by the police, and read a paper to him, containing, as she said, the testimony which she had given on the examination, which she had written down herself.
After reading the paper through, she told him that Strang had said, he would have her if it cost him his life—and proposed going to Canada with her.

Did not recollect, certainly, whether she had previously read this to him, but was certain, if she had, that she repeated it afterwards. Witness becoming convinced of her guilt, discontinued his visits to her in about a fortnight.

This witness was long and closely examined by Mr. Williams, but the purport of his testimony was not varied, nor any new facts elicited, except that the witness had often said that he believed her guilty of the death of his uncle, and if she was guilty, he hoped she would be hanged.

Witness was 23 years old last May; he is a son of William Whipple, who lived at Cazenovia, Madison county; he came to Albany on May 5; put up at Fobes’ in Albany, and then went to Barnum Whipple’s; don't know if Barnum Whipple’s wife was at Cherry Hill on a certain day after the murder; has been at B. Whipple’s ever since; has told Barnum that prisoner said she could swear Orton was innocent; has told him more than once and believes within a fortnight after W. was shot; witness did not go before the Grand Jury; Barnum told him not to go; Barnum said he did not want witness to swear before the grand jury; nor to tell any one who would make him swear to it. The next person whom he told as to what Mrs. Whipple said, was Mr. Shaffer; cannot tell whether he told it before or after Strang’s trial was finished; he thinks he told part of it before it was finished; this was in witness’ victualling cellar in State street; went into business here on June 6, went to Cherry Hill every day for a fortnight after the murder, sometimes two or three times a day; has eat at the same table with prisoner, but whether more than once or not, can’t say; Miss Patrick was at the table once in prisoner’s presence; witness had a conversation once with prisoner on the front steps, when Mrs. Barnum Whipple was present; at one time Mrs. Whipple said she hoped they would not hang Orton without judge or jury; witness told Shaffer he heard Mrs. Whipple say she would swear Strang was innocent; also told Shaffer about Mrs. Whipple getting the money at Fobes’; told Shaffer part to day, in the crowd, and Shaffer told witness he must not go off. Prisoner once took witness into her bed room, and read the oath which she said she had taken before Mr. Cole and the Mayor; don’t recollect what she said. — At one of the conversations, prisoner told witness that Strang had said he would have her if it cost him his life, and that he proposed taking her to Canada. Witness thinks she read this in her affidavit; don’t recollect that she ever said any thing about her aunt Catharine Van Rensselaer.

Witness thinks prisoner is guilty and may have so expressed himself; he has often said if she was guilty, she ought to be hung. — The reason why witness did not before tell all he knew was that he did not wish to be called on as a witness; when he told Mr. Shaffer, he thought he would not be called on as a witness; don’t know, but he has told what he knew to others besides his uncle Barnum and Mr. Shaffer.

lines: At 6 o’clock the District Attorney moved the court that Jesse Strang be called to the stand to testify.
Mr. Livingston called for Jesse Strang.
By the court. You cannot call Strang upon the stand without an order from the court, Mr. Livingston then moved that Jesse Strang be called into court to testify in this cause.

Mr. Van Vechten, on behalf of the prisoner, objected, inasmuch as Strang had been convicted as principal, of an infamous crime, and was therefore by law rendered incompetent as a witness to testify in any cause.

Mr. Van Vechten also contended that if used as a witness he must become a subject of executive clemency. Mr. Van Vechten having opened the argument upon the objection, and cited two or three authorities, said the counsel for the prisoner would reserve themselves until after the counsel for the prosecution should have been heard in support of the motion.

The District Attorney spoke in reply, and in regard to the first objection, contended that it is not the conviction for an infamous crime, but the sentence, which creates the disqualification. In the present case, the sentence had not yet been pronounced, and Strang is therefore a competent witness.

As it regarded the second point, viz., the claims which being used as a witness would give Strang to a pardon, the District Attorney maintained that it did not necessarily follow; that would be a subject altogether for the consideration of the executive.
He must act upon his own responsibility, and judge whether the circumstances would in any respect render it his duty to extend his clemency.

Mr. Livingston did not hesitate to express his opinion upon the subject, and he had consulted able counsel, and his conviction was, that if Strang should be called upon the stand, and was solemnly premonished that he need not under any circumstances hope for a pardon in this world (as was done in the case of Hodges, in Orange County) he would not be entitled to any mercy whatever.
It being now past 8 o'clock the court directed a recess until to-morrow morning, at 10 o'clock, when the opinion upon this important question will be pronounced.
THE PEOPLE v. ELISE WHIPPLE

On the opening of the court this morning, Judge Duer pronounced the opinion of the court upon the question raised and argued last night, whether Strang, the principal in the felony, and wherewith the accused stood charged as an accessory, should be admitted to testify against the accused.

The Judges stated, that upon examination of the authorities, the court had come to the conclusion that there was no doubt but that a person, though convicted of a crime, is a competent witness in all cases, until the judgment upon that conviction is pronounced against him.

It has been said that the common opinion was, that a conviction alone rendered him incompetent; but that, the court said, was not the law. It is not the conviction, but the judgment, that creates the disability in such cases.

As an accomplice, Strang is a competent witness. Unless the conviction and judgment are proved, a witness is not incompetent from infamy of character, though he may confess himself guilty of an infamous crime.

This case then addressed itself to the discretion of the court, not to their judgment as to the competency of the witness, but to their discretion whether, on a principle of public policy, and in furtherance of public justice, the person convicted shall be permitted to testify against the accused.

From the evidence before the court, it appeared that Strang meditated the murder he committed for the space of six months; that he had an illicit intercourse with the prisoner at the bar; and that he had expressed himself determined to have her if it cost him his life.
He is a man of about 30 years of age, not deficient in experience, on the contrary artful and deceptive, passing himself off as an unmarried man, and under a false and assumed name.

The character in which he appears before the court as to his participation in the crime which has been committed, is not as an instrument used by the prisoner to get rid of her husband, but the seducer of the prisoner to obtain possession of her person and property.

The prisoner at the bar appears as a young woman, now about 25 years of age, married at the early age of 14 to her late husband, possessed of property to a considerable amount, of a character light, frivolous, weak, vain, imprudent and wicked, and guilty to a certain degree; a fit instrument in the hands of a designing man, but destitute of those qualities which might be supposed to have swayed the mind or controlled the actions of the person with whom she had had an illicit intercourse.

Had the case been reversed, and she presented as a woman of experience, of strength of mind and energy of character, who had lived unhappily with her husband, and expressed a determination to get rid of him—who had selected as her paramour a youth of inexperience, and by the seductions of her person and her fortune had induced him to commit the murder, in the exercise of their discretion the court would not have hesitated to admit him as a witness, and in a full disclosure of the facts to have recommended him to mercy.
The Judge therefore decided that Jesse Strang cannot be admitted as a witness.

After a few moments, the district attorney arose and observed, that as the testimony already produced would not warrant the jury in convicting the prisoner, and inasmuch as under the decision of the court the testimony of Strang could not be admitted, he would abandon the prosecution.
Judge Duer.

That is a matter in the discretion of the public prosecutor, and the court will not attempt to control him in the exercise of that discretion, but they apprise the public prosecutor that if a motion had been made by the counsel of the prisoner, for her discharge on the ground of want of testimony, the motion would have been denied. If the testimony which remained was of a slight nature, it might have been cause for resting the prosecution upon the evidence already adduced; but not for discharging the prisoner.
Robert Livingston, DA
Under this intimation from the court without having changed my opinion. I wish to be considered as resting the prosecution, and call upon the prisoner for her defence.
Mr. Foot.

There is some difference of opinion, perfectly kind and friendly however, between the District Attorney and myself. In consequence of the suggestions of the court he now appears to be willing to put the prisoner on her defence. Satisfied myself that she cannot and ought not to be convicted upon the testimony given, and which is still in the power of the public prosecutor to produce, I have advised that the prosecution be abandoned, considering the intimation of the court only as an expression of opinion that in a criminal case the jury should be permitted to pronounce upon the evidence, instead of stopping the trial by the court, as is done in civil cases when there is a defeat of testimony.

Mr. Van Vechten observed, that after the candid admissions made by the counsel for the prosecution, the counsel for the prisoner would not call any witnesses, though they had it in their power to show strong explanatory testimony, and would submit the case to the charge of the court.

Judge Duer, after adverting to what had just transpired, and without recapitulating the testimony, submitted the case to the consideration of the jury. He cautioned them to look only at the evidence which affected the guilt or innocence of the prisoner in relation to the charge for which she was upon trial.

As to the evidence which had been adduced, showing her guilt in other respects, he advised them to say to her, as the court were disposed to say, and as the Saviour of the world said upon another occasion, "Go, and sin no more."
The jury, without leaving their seats, found a verdict of NOT GUILTY.
Again an expression of approbation was manifested; but it was immediately restrained. The unfortunate prisoner received the verdict of the jury, leaning forward, her face resting upon the table.

She neither looked up, nor seemed to be moved by the abrupt transition in the aspect of the trial which followed the decision of the court; nor did she appear to be particularly affected upon the rendering of the verdict, though she held her handkerchief to her face and wept; and when, under the proper and strong admonition of the court, that no unfeeling and curious eye should attempt to penetrate the thick veil which concealed her countenance from general observation, she left the chamber, she seemed to move mechanically and by the attending officers, rather than by any volition of her own.
Friday, August 3, 1827
The Troy Sentinel
THE TRIAL OF MRS. WHIPPLE

On Monday last, about 1 o'clock this wretched woman was brought again to the bar and the whole of the remainder of the day was continued in completing the panel of jurors. On Tuesday, at 9 o'clock the trial was opened, the court stating to the jury that the prisoner, Elsie D. Whipple, stood indicted for a felony, as accessary, before the fact, to the murder of her husband John Whipple; and the District Attorney reading the indictment, and stating the facts which he should give in evidence. When the first witness on the part of the prosecution, was called, Mr. Van Vechten, of counsel for the prisoner, objected that before any testimony could be offered to prove that the prisoner was accessary, the conviction of the principal must be legally proved, which, he contended, could not be done in any other way, than by exhibiting the record of the conviction of the principal. The objection was argued by counsel, and sustained by the court. After some little delay, a record of the trial of Strang with the verdict of guilty entered thereon, was then produced. Mr. E. Williams, also of counsel for the prisoner, then objected that the record was not sufficient without setting forth the sentence, and he cited authorities. This objection, however, after solemn argument was overruled, and the examination of witnesses was resumed.

While the first witness Abram L. Van Rensselaer was under examination, the District Attorney offered him, for his perusal to refresh his memory, an affidavit which he had made before a police justice, some time after the facts took place. Upon the objection of counsel that this was not a memorandum made at the time, but written down by a magistrate upon an ex parte examination, and, therefore, not such a paper as a witness might refer to, the court decided that the paper could not be used; and the examination proceeded. Three other witnesses were examined, and the court adjourned till the next morning.

The progress of the trial was interrupted, on Wednesday afternoon, by the appearance, in the N.Y. American and N.Y. Com. Advertiser, of the report of the trial of Strang at full length, contrary to an order of the court heretofore noticed, that no report of either trial should be published until both should be finished.

Upon the evidence being presented to the court of the violation of this order, the Judge made an order that Charles King and William L. Stone appear before the court and shew cause why an attachment should not be issued against them for contempt of court.
